name: Erik Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't go with any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Greystone, the Hartley family's farm outside Upton Moor: a hundred and twenty milking cows, wheat and grass for silage. I'm in the parlour at half four with Will Hartley, then I scrape the yards, bed the cubicles and feed the calves. In spring and summer I'm on the silage clamp, rolling it with the old tractor. I like the early mornings and the cows' routine, and I hate how slow I still am at spotting a lame cow.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at Greystone?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years. I drove lorries for twenty years, long distance, until a slipped disc put me off the road for good. John Hartley knows me from chapel, and he gave me a start when nobody else would. My wife Teresa does school dinners, and we've got Daniel, who's fourteen, Grace, who's ten, and a mortgage on a house on Church Lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, and I'd say it at the chapel tea. I've never touched these AI things and never wanted to. People should be working with their hands and their heads, not asking a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, my worry isn't AI, it's the milk price and Will's robot. Will Hartley priced up a milking robot last spring, the old kind that's been around for years, and the bank said maybe next year. A milking robot doesn't need any of this AI business to take my job, it just needs a bank loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and make myself useful in ways a milking box can't, like calving and the silage. I'd ask John Hartley straight whether the robot's coming, man to man. And we'd cut back, maybe drop the satellite telly and the second phone contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach, but I'd pray on it. I've been knocked down before, with the back. I'd take it a day at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your back hold up with farm work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some days fine, some days I'm on painkillers by ten. I can't lift like the young lads. That's partly why the robot worries me, because I can't just go labouring somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Teresa think about the robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teresa says trust the Lord and trust John Hartley, in that order. Teresa's probably right. But Teresa's not the one being replaced by a box on legs.

say: I'd say **I told you so** at the chapel tea.
I'd say people should work with **their hands and heads**, not ask a phone.
think: I think the real threat is **Will's milking robot**, which needs no AI at all.
I think it only needs a **bank loan**, and the bank said maybe next year.
do: Make myself useful at **calving and silage**, where a milking box can't help.
Ask **John Hartley** straight whether the robot's coming.
Drop the **satellite telly** and the second phone contract.
feel: He feels **uneasy** in his stomach and would **pray** on it.
S0.quote: A milking robot doesn't need any of this AI business to take my job, it just needs a bank loan.
fieldNote: His threat predates AI: an ordinary **milking robot** the Hartleys have already priced.
His **bad back** rules out other labouring jobs, which deepens the worry.
He leans on **faith and loyalty** to John Hartley from chapel.

steps.text: Take on more calving and silage work beside the milking
Drop the satellite telly and the second phone contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of fuss about office work, and good luck to them. Farming's farming. I'd say young people should get a trade instead of sitting at screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry the clever stuff makes Will's robot cheaper and smarter. If the computer can plan the feed and the breeding, Will needs one man less, and I'm the newest. Last in, first out, that's fair, but it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't touch the AI stuff, I'll be straight with you. I'd ask John to put me forward for the cattle foot-trimming course, because that's a trade. I'd pick up extra on Saturdays helping Mr Okoro next door with his sheep, if he'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like the day the doctor said no more driving. You know something's shifted. You just don't know how far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said last in, first out is fair. Do you really think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do, yes, that's how it should work. It doesn't mean I'd like it. I'd shake Will Hartley's hand on the way out and then go home and kick the shed door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the Hartleys, they're doing their best. I'd blame the big companies and the government in the city who make everything cheaper than farmers can make it. That's what squeezes Will into buying the robot.

say: I'd say it's **fuss about office work** and farming's farming.
I'd tell young people to **get a trade**.
think: I think smarter AI makes **Will's robot** cheaper and smarter.
I think I'm **last in, first out**, and that's me.
do: Ask John for the **foot-trimming course**, because it's a trade.
Pick up Saturday work with **Mr Okoro's sheep**.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, like the day the doctor said **no more driving**.
S1.quote: I'd shake Will Hartley's hand on the way out and then go home and kick the shed door.
fieldNote: He accepts **last in, first out** as fair while dreading it.
He blames **big companies and government**, never the Hartleys.
His answer to change is **a trade**, like foot trimming, not technology.

steps.text: Ask John Hartley for a place on the foot-trimming course
Offer Saturday help with Mr Okoro's sheep next door

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say God help us, and I'd mean it. I'd say whoever let this happen so fast should answer for it. At chapel I'd ask people to pray for the families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the thinking machines run the farm office, and by 2031 there's a robot that can milk, scrape and calve. I can't drive lorries with my back, and I can't use a computer. In two years I'd be a man with a bad back, no computer skills and nothing left to offer Greystone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. I'd cut everything, and I'd talk to the pastor and my brother Luis about help. I'd ask John Hartley to keep me on as long as he can, and I'd keep turning up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, if I'm honest. I've got no plan for this one. I'd be lying awake, and I'd be short with Teresa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's football boots and the trip to Teresa's mother at Easter. Then the car insurance down to the cheapest. After that I don't know, there's not much left to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your brother Luis do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis would help with a few hundred, and he'd tell me to come work at his tyre shop. My back couldn't take tyres all day. I'd go anyway, because that's what you do for your family.

say: I'd say **God help us** and that someone should **answer** for it.
I'd ask the chapel to **pray for the families**.
think: I think a robot can **milk, scrape and calve** by 2031.
I think with my **bad back** and no computer skills, I'd have nothing left.
do: Cut **everything**, starting with Daniel's football boots.
Ask the pastor and my brother **Luis** for help.
Keep **turning up** and ask John to keep me on.
feel: He feels **panicked**, with **no plan** for this one.
He'd lie awake and be **short with Teresa**.
S2.quote: In two years I'd be a man with a bad back, no computer skills and nothing left to offer Greystone.
fieldNote: Every exit is closed to him: the **bad back** rules out labour and he refuses computers.
He has **no plan** and no savings, only family and chapel.
He'd take **Luis's tyre shop** job despite the back, out of duty.

steps.text: Ask the pastor and my brother Luis for help
Cancel Daniel's football boots and the Easter trip
Keep turning up at Greystone until John lets me go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and men should get learning a trade now. At chapel I'd tell the younger ones not to waste it. I wouldn't go online, I don't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the same end, but I'd have five years to find something my back can stand. Robots by 2034 means I'm fifty-one and the kids nearly grown. Five more years at Greystone would see Daniel through school, and that's all I'd ask of the Lord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the foot-trimming course and then the hoof care certificate, because cows will need feet seen to by a person longest. I'd save the Saturday money from Mr Okoro's sheep. I'd still not touch the computers, but I'd let Daniel show me the basics if he'd be patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but less. Five years is a long time to a man who's had to start again once already. I'd still lie awake some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let Daniel show you the computer. That's new.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, isn't it. I'd do it for the job, not because I like it. And Daniel would enjoy bossing me about, I expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from outside, from government or anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper apprenticeships for men my age, paid, not a handout. And the government should stop the big companies flooding the market with cheap food. That's what makes the farmers buy robots.

say: I'd tell men to **learn a trade now**.
I'd tell the younger ones at chapel **not to waste** the five years.
think: I think five years gives time to find work my **back can stand**.
I think robots at fifty-one leave the **kids nearly grown**.
do: Do the **foot-trimming course** and then the hoof care certificate.
Save the **Saturday sheep money** from Mr Okoro.
feel: He feels **frightened, but less**, and still lies awake some nights.
S3.quote: Five more years at Greystone would see Daniel through school, and that's all I'd ask of the Lord.
fieldNote: Five years moves him from no plan to a **hoof care trade** he thinks will last.
He'd let his son teach him **computers**, a small shift for a resistant man.
He asks for **paid apprenticeships**, not handouts, and blames cheap food imports.

steps.text: Take the foot-trimming course, then the hoof care certificate
Save the Saturday money from Mr Okoro's sheep
Let Daniel teach me computer basics on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair chance, and anyone who doesn't take it has only themselves to blame. I'd say that at chapel and mean it. A man can learn a lot in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years plus three takes me to fifty-six, and Daniel and Grace would be grown. I could be a hoof trimmer with my own round by then. With ten years, a lorry driver with a bad back can still build a trade the robots won't want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the foot-trimming course this winter and build up a few farms as customers over the years. I'd pay off the car and get a month put by. I'd keep working at Greystone as long as the Hartleys want me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, though still careful. It's a chance, not a promise. I'd still say my prayers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years make you try the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for the bookings, if my own hoof round got busy. I'd want Grace to set it up, she's better than Daniel. But I'd keep a paper diary too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the robots learn hoof trimming too. Then it's all for nothing. But I'd take the chance.

say: I'd say ten years is a **fair chance** for anyone willing.
I'd say a man can **learn a lot** in ten years.
think: I think by fifty-six I could run **my own hoof round**.
I think a trade **the robots won't want** is still possible.
do: Pay off the car and get **a month put by**.
Keep working at **Greystone** as long as the Hartleys want me.
feel: He feels **calmer** but careful: it's **a chance**, not a promise.
S4.quote: With ten years, a lorry driver with a bad back can still build a trade the robots won't want.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him plan a **self-employed trade**, which fits his free-market views.
He'd accept AI only for **bookings**, set up by his daughter Grace.
He fears robots may **learn hoof trimming** too, but would still take the chance.

steps.text: Start the foot-trimming course this winter
Pay off the car and save a month of expenses
Keep working at Greystone while building a hoof round

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no trade, no back for labouring and no savings, all at once. What would help is a paid apprenticeship for men my age, in something like hoof care. I don't want charity, I want a trade I can still do with a bad back at fifty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. My faith's what got me through the back injury. It would get me through this too, one way or another.

headlineQuote: I don't want charity, I want a trade I can still do with a bad back at fifty.
portrait: Erik is a **former lorry driver** who joined the Hartleys' dairy farm after a slipped disc ended his driving.
He never uses **AI tools**, distrusts them, and still struggles to spot a lame cow.
He fears **Will's milking robot** even in the mildest picture, and turns **panicked** when AGI comes in two years.
He leans on **chapel, family** and loyalty to the Hartleys, and refuses handouts.
With more time, he plans a **hoof care trade** and his own round of farms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no trade, no back for labour and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** for men his age, in a trade like **hoof care**.
